question: How many pairs of shoes did Adidas manufacture worldwide in 2023?
context: Pairs, not individual shoes. Include production by manufacturing partners.
route: Start with the number of people who buy athletic shoes, their replacement cycle, and the fraction choosing this brand. Allow for shoes made but not yet sold.
example: For example: 2 billion potential buyers × 1 pair per year × a 15% brand share ≈ 300 million pairs. These are illustrative guesses, not reported market shares.
insight: A purchase that feels occasional becomes a huge production flow when multiplied across a worldwide customer base.

question: How many pairs of Adidas shoes were made in Vietnam in 2023?
context: Adidas footwear only; pairs, not individual shoes.
route: Estimate worldwide demand for the brand, then the share supplied by Vietnam. Think about athletic-shoe buyers and how much manufacturing is concentrated in a few countries.
example: One rough route: 2 billion buyers × 1 pair/year × 15% brand share × one-third made in Vietnam ≈ 100 million pairs. The report instead gives 311 million pairs globally and a 38% Vietnam share.
insight: The published country share is rounded, so the reference is an approximate allocation of output, not an exact factory count.

question: How many items of clothing did Adidas manufacture worldwide in 2023?
context: Apparel, including manufacturing partners; exclude shoes and accessories.
route: Think about the worldwide customer base, how often people replace sportswear, and the fraction of those purchases supplied by Adidas.
example: A rough model: 1 billion sportswear buyers × 3 items/year × a 10% brand share ≈ 300 million items. Actual production also reflects inventory changes.
insight: Clothing units are individual items, unlike footwear reported in pairs.

question: How many pieces of mail and packages did the US Postal Service deliver in fiscal 2024?
context: October 2023–September 2024. Include letters, advertising mail and packages.
route: Picture a mailbox over a week. Multiply pieces per delivery day by delivery days and the number of household and business addresses.
example: An illustrative estimate: 150 million addresses × 2.5 pieces/day × 300 delivery days ≈ 112.5 billion pieces. Those inputs are rounded assumptions; the postal total is reported separately.
insight: Advertising and business mail matter: counting only parcels would miss most of this flow.

question: How many packages did the US Postal Service handle in fiscal 2024?
context: October 2023–September 2024. Shipping and packages category; exclude letters and advertising mail.
route: Estimate households, packages per household per week, and the postal service share of deliveries. Add business shipments and returns.
example: For scale: 130 million households × 2 packages/week × 52 weeks × a half carried by USPS ≈ 6.76 billion packages, before business traffic.
insight: The carrier share matters as much as how frequently you personally order online.

question: How many express parcels did China’s courier sector handle in 2024?
context: Express courier parcels; not the broader total for all postal services.
route: Estimate how many people shop online, how frequently they order, and parcels per order. Include business traffic and returns.
example: One possible estimate: 1 billion shoppers × 3 parcels/week × 52 ≈ 156 billion parcels. Non-shopping shipments and split orders can push the total higher.
insight: Order frequency is a stronger lever than the size of a single purchase.

question: How many food and drink packages did Tetra Pak sell worldwide in 2023?
context: Individual packages, not litres; include all sizes.
route: Start with people who regularly buy carton-packed drinks or food. Estimate weekly packages and the share supplied by this packaging company.
example: For illustration: 4 billion users × 1 package/week × 52 × an 80% supplier share ≈ 166 billion packages. These are scale estimates, not measured shares.
insight: Small single-serving cartons and large family cartons each count as one package.

question: How many meatballs, plant balls and veggie balls did IKEA sell in its US restaurants in fiscal 2025?
sourceName: IKEA US · Annual Summary FY25, p.38
context: US restaurants only; all three types combined. September 2024–August 2025.
route: Estimate annual store visits, the fraction who eat a ball-based meal, and balls per plate. Do not count every visitor as a diner.
example: For example: 60 million store visits × 8% ordering a ball meal × 8 balls ≈ 38.4 million balls. The dining share and serving size are illustrative.
insight: A restaurant inside a furniture store can operate at the scale of a large food business.

question: How many motor vehicles were manufactured worldwide in 2023?
context: Passenger cars and commercial vehicles; exclude motorcycles. Use OICA’s 2023 table.
route: Estimate the existing vehicle fleet and how long vehicles last, then add growth in ownership and commercial fleets.
example: A rough replacement model: 1.4 billion vehicles ÷ 18 years ≈ 78 million replacements/year. Adding 15 million for fleet growth gives roughly 93 million. These are illustrative inputs.
insight: Annual production replaces old vehicles as well as supplying new drivers.

question: How much electronic waste did the world generate in 2022?
context: Discarded electrical and electronic equipment, including large appliances. Weight, not item count.
route: Inventory devices and appliances used by a household. Divide their combined mass by their useful lifetimes, scale to households, and add commercial equipment.
example: An illustrative household model: 200 kg of equipment replaced over 10 years × 3 billion households ≈ 60 million tonnes/year. Business equipment and uneven ownership complicate this.
insight: Phones draw attention, but refrigerators, washing machines and other heavy equipment dominate many waste streams.

question: How many servings of Coca-Cola Company drinks were consumed worldwide per day in 2023?
context: All company brands, including water and juice. A serving is 8 US fluid ounces (about 237 ml), not necessarily a bottle.
route: Estimate how many people drink one of the company’s brands daily, then the average number of serving-sized portions they consume.
example: For scale: 8 billion people × one-quarter drinking these brands on a given day × 1 serving ≈ 2 billion daily servings. Larger bottles can contain multiple servings.
insight: Brand scope and portion size change the answer enormously.

question: How many visits did the Louvre receive in 2023?
context: Museum visits, not unique people or visits to the surrounding gardens.
route: Estimate people admitted per hour, opening hours, and open days. Check the result against a plausible daily crowd.
example: An illustrative throughput estimate: 3,000 admissions/hour × 9 hours × 300 open days ≈ 8.1 million visits. Peak days and evening openings change the total.
insight: A visitor total is a flow through the building, not the number standing inside at once.

question: How many scheduled airline departures took place worldwide in 2023?
context: Scheduled services, worldwide. Each flight leg counts once; exclude private and military flying.
route: Estimate the active airline fleet and flights per aircraft per day. Allow for long-haul aircraft and aircraft out of service.
example: For example: 25,000 aircraft × 4 departures/day × 350 operating days ≈ 35 million departures. This is an illustrative fleet model.
insight: One connecting journey produces multiple flight legs, while each leg carries many passengers.

question: How many hours of Netflix did people watch worldwide during 2023?
sourceName: Netflix · What We Watched, second half of 2023
context: Total viewing time across films and series; not the number of completed titles.
route: Estimate subscribing households, average daily viewing time per household, and days in the year. Account for households that rarely watch.
example: For example: 250 million households × 2 hours/day × 365 ≈ 182.5 billion hours. This is a household viewing model, not an assertion about the average individual.
insight: Many simultaneous viewers turn ordinary evening habits into billions of hours.

question: How much food waste did households worldwide generate in 2022?
sourceName: UNEP · Food Waste Index 2024 key messages
context: Households only. Include inedible parts such as peels and bones; exclude restaurants and shops.
route: Picture the daily food scraps and uneaten food from one person. Convert that to an annual amount and scale to the world.
example: As a rough model: 8 billion people × 0.2 kg/day × 365 ≈ 584 million tonnes/year. The daily amount is an estimation assumption.
insight: Peels, bones and leftovers all count here, so this is broader than edible food thrown away.

question: How much crude steel did the world produce in 2023?
sourceName: World Steel Association · World Steel in Figures 2024
context: Crude steel before finishing into products. Use the rounded 2024 report figure.
route: Think beyond cars: estimate steel for new buildings and infrastructure, then add vehicles, machinery and appliances. Cross-check against an annual amount per person.
example: A rough per-person check: 8 billion people × 250 kg of new steel/year ≈ 2 billion tonnes. That allowance includes shared infrastructure, not just possessions.
insight: Buildings and infrastructure can outweigh the metal you see in household products.

question: How many passenger journeys passed through Heathrow Airport in 2023?
context: Arrivals and departures combined, as reported by the airport; not unique travellers.
route: Estimate daily arriving and departing flights, seats per plane, and the fraction of seats filled.
example: For example: 1,200 flight movements/day × 200 passengers/movement × 365 ≈ 87.6 million passenger journeys. Aircraft mix and empty seats reduce this.
insight: Do not double an estimate that already includes both arriving and departing flights.

question: How much drinking water does New York City’s water system supply to the city in a typical day?
sourceName: NYC Department of Environmental Protection · water supply
context: Use DEP’s rounded daily supply estimate for NYC. Include household and business uses, not just water people drink.
route: Estimate residents and daily water per resident for showers, toilets, laundry and cooking. Add offices, restaurants and system losses.
example: One rough model: 8 million residents × 300 litres/day ≈ 2.4 billion litres, plus about a billion litres for businesses and other uses.
insight: The phrase drinking water describes water quality; most of it is used for washing, flushing and other purposes.

question: How many recreational visits were recorded across the US National Park System in 2023?
context: All reporting National Park System sites, including monuments and recreation areas; not just parks named “National Park.”
route: Estimate how many people visit these sites each year and how many visits they make. Include nearby recreation areas and repeated visits.
example: For example: 150 million domestic and overseas visitors × 2 visits each ≈ 300 million visits. Visitors and repeats are illustrative assumptions.
insight: Restricting your estimate to the famous wilderness parks misses many local recreation sites.

question: How much honey did US beekeepers produce in 2023?
context: US production from operations with five or more colonies; exclude imported honey.
route: Estimate honey consumption from jars bought per household, then separate domestic production from imports. A hive-count × yield cross-check also works.
example: One household model: 130 million households × 1 kg/year × a half supplied domestically ≈ 65 million kg. These are rough assumptions, not consumption statistics.
insight: Honey on a US supermarket shelf is not necessarily produced by US bees.

question: How much maple syrup did the United States produce in 2023?
sourceName: USDA NASS · 2024 Maple Syrup Survey announcement
context: US maple syrup production, not sap and not maple-flavoured pancake syrup. Use the published 2023 estimate.
route: Estimate households buying real maple syrup, bottles per year and bottle volume. Allow for Canadian imports and food-service demand.
example: For scale: 40 million households × 2 half-litre bottles/year × a 40% US-produced share ≈ 16 million litres. These are illustrative demand assumptions.
insight: Most pancake syrups are a different product; including them would greatly inflate this estimate.

question: How many trees were estimated to exist on Earth in the 2015 global tree census study?
context: The study’s global estimate of trees with trunks larger than 10 cm in diameter; not seedlings.
route: Estimate forested area and trees in a patch you can picture. Scale trees per hectare, allowing for open woodland and dense forests.
example: An illustrative check: 40 million km² of forest × 75,000 trees/km² ≈ 3 trillion trees. That density is 750 trees per hectare; it is a scale check, not the study’s method.
insight: Different forest types have very different densities, so a single familiar forest is an uncertain guide.

question: How many ants were estimated to live on Earth in the 2022 global abundance study?
context: Use the paper’s conservative global estimate of living ants, not species or colonies.
route: Picture ants in a square metre of suitable habitat, including colonies below the surface. Scale over habitable land and allow for large differences between habitats.
example: For scale: 100 million km² × 1 million m²/km² × 200 ants/m² ≈ 20 quadrillion ants. This average is illustrative, not a claim that every square metre contains 200 ants.
insight: Tiny animals become a planetary-scale population when both colony size and habitat area are considered.

question: How many times does the International Space Station circle Earth in 24 hours?
context: Use NASA’s rounded orbital rate, not Earth’s daily rotation.
route: Estimate the distance around Earth and the station’s speed. Divide to get an orbit time, then compare with a full day.
example: For scale: roughly 40,000 km around Earth ÷ roughly 28,000 km/hour ≈ 1.4 hours per circuit; allowing for altitude gives roughly 16 circuits per day.
insight: An astronaut’s orbital day is much shorter than the day on the ground.

question: How much Moon rock and soil did all the Apollo landing missions bring back to Earth?
context: All crewed Apollo lunar landings combined; exclude later robotic missions and meteorites.
route: Estimate the number of landings, then what two astronauts could collect and fit into sample containers on each mission. Later missions carried more.
example: An illustrative estimate: 6 missions × 60 kg per mission ≈ 360 kg. The per-mission amount varied substantially; the published total is 382 kg.
insight: Returning samples requires launch capacity as well as the time to collect them.

question: How many commercial satellites were deployed into orbit worldwide in 2023?
context: Commercial satellites only. Count satellites, not rocket launches.
route: Estimate launches carrying commercial payloads, then satellites per launch. Large communications constellations put many small satellites on one rocket.
example: For illustration: 100 launches carrying 25 small satellites plus 100 single-payload launches ≈ 2,600 satellites. Actual launch mixes differ.
insight: A launch count is no longer a close proxy for a satellite count.

question: How many rivets were used to construct the Eiffel Tower?
context: All construction rivets, including those fitted in the workshop.
route: Imagine the tower as thousands of metal pieces joined at both ends. Estimate pieces, connections per piece and rivets per connection; avoid double-counting shared joints.
example: An illustrative route: 20,000 pieces × 2 ends × 60 rivets per end ≈ 2.4 million rivets. Joint details vary, so this is only a scale model.
insight: Most of the rivets were fitted before the pieces reached the tower.

question: How much paint is needed for a full repainting of the Eiffel Tower?
context: Use the operator’s standard repainting-campaign estimate; paint applied, not accumulated old paint.
route: Estimate the exposed surface area of the metalwork, coverage per litre and paint mass per litre. Both sides of many beams need coating.
example: For example: 250,000 m² × 0.2 litres/m² × 1.2 kg/litre ≈ 60,000 kg. Coverage and density here are illustrative; the operator reports about 60 tonnes.
insight: An open lattice has much more paintable surface than its silhouette suggests.

question: How long was the Union Pacific–Central Pacific rail link completed in 1869?
sourceName: US National Archives · the Golden Spike
context: The newly joined route from the Omaha/Council Bluffs area to Sacramento; not the entire coast-to-coast network.
route: Picture the western portion of the United States on a map. Estimate its east–west span, then add distance for a route through passes and valleys.
example: A rough map estimate: 2,400 km straight across this region × 1.2 for the railway’s route ≈ 2,880 km.
insight: A route called transcontinental did not mean all of the coast-to-coast track was newly built in 1869.

question: How much concrete is in Hoover Dam itself?
sourceName: US Bureau of Reclamation · Hoover Dam
context: The dam body only; exclude the powerplant and other associated structures.
route: Picture a canyon-wide wall that is very thick at the bottom and narrow at the top. Estimate its average cross-section and length.
example: An illustrative wedge: 200 m high × 60 m average thickness × 200 m effective average span ≈ 2.4 million m³. A real curved dam has a more complicated geometry.
insight: Using the base thickness everywhere would greatly overestimate the amount of concrete.

question: How many physical books did UK publishers sell in 2022?
context: UK publishing industry sales, including exports and educational books. Not just books bought by UK residents.
route: Estimate domestic consumer purchases, school and academic demand, then add exports to the much larger English-language market.
example: For scale: 70 million domestic readers × 5 books/year ≈ 350 million books; an export and institutional contribution of a similar order puts the total in the hundreds of millions.
insight: Publisher location and reader location are different things: exports are a major part of this total.

question: How much aquatic animal life did fisheries and fish farms produce worldwide in 2022?
sourceName: FAO · State of World Fisheries and Aquaculture 2024
context: Live-weight equivalent of aquatic animals, including shellfish; exclude algae. Include farmed and wild-caught production.
route: Estimate fish and shellfish eaten per person per year. Scale to the world, then allow for bones, shells, losses and non-food uses.
example: For example: 8 billion people × 15 kg of edible seafood/year ÷ a 65% usable fraction ≈ 185 million tonnes of live weight. Those are illustrative assumptions, not the FAO calculation.
insight: Fillet weight and whole-animal weight are not interchangeable.

question: How many packages did UPS deliver worldwide in 2023?
context: UPS packages worldwide, including business deliveries and returns; exclude other carriers.
route: Estimate delivery routes, stops per route, packages per stop and delivery days. Think about commercial addresses receiving several packages.
example: An illustrative route model: 100,000 routes × 200 packages/day × 280 days ≈ 5.6 billion packages. These inputs are guesses, not reported fleet statistics.
insight: Route productivity provides another way to estimate a market without knowing the number of shoppers.

question: How many tennis balls are used during a Wimbledon tournament?
context: Use the LTA’s approximate two-week tournament total, including practice.
route: Estimate matches across all draws, games per match, ball changes and balls per change. Add practice sessions.
example: For illustration: 700 matches × 4 batches × 6 balls ≈ 16,800 match balls. Practice across many courts adds tens of thousands more.
insight: Counting only the singles finals leaves out nearly all tournament activity.

question: How much strawberry fruit was eaten at Wimbledon in 2022?
sourceName: Wimbledon · Food and Drink 2023 fact sheet, p.1
context: Fruit weight only; exclude cream. The 2023 fact sheet reports the 2022 tournament.
route: Estimate daily spectators, tournament days, the fraction buying strawberries, and fruit per serving. Include staff and hospitality.
example: For scale: 40,000 visits/day × 14 days × half buying 0.15 kg ≈ 42,000 kg, before staff and hospitality. These are illustrative assumptions.
insight: The year on a report cover can differ from the year of the numbers inside.

question: How many stadium admissions were recorded across the 2022 men’s football World Cup?
context: All matches combined; repeat spectators count again. Use FIFA’s rounded summary figure.
route: Reconstruct the number of matches from the group stage and knockout bracket, then estimate average crowd size.
example: The format gives 48 group games plus 16 knockout/placement games = 64. An average crowd of 50,000 would give 3.2 million admissions.
insight: Repeat attendance is essential: this is not a count of people who travelled to Qatar.

question: How many eggs were produced in the United States in the 2023 USDA reporting year?
sourceName: USDA NASS · Poultry Production and Value 2024 summary
context: Year ending November 30, 2023. Include table and hatching eggs; use the rounded published total.
route: Estimate eggs eaten per person, including baking and prepared foods, then add hatching eggs and losses.
example: For scale: 330 million people × 300 eggs/year ≈ 99 billion eggs. Hatching eggs and other differences between production and consumption add to that.
insight: The carton in your fridge is only part of egg demand: bakeries and food manufacturers also use large volumes.

question: How much wine was produced worldwide in 2023?
context: Wine, not grapes or grape juice. Use OIV’s April 2024 production estimate.
route: Estimate the number of regular wine consumers and bottles per year, then account for occasional consumers and changes in stored wine.
example: For example: 1 billion consumers × 30 bottles/year × 0.75 litres ≈ 22.5 billion litres. This is a consumption-based scale check; production and consumption differ.
insight: A harvest year can change production substantially even when habits change slowly.

question: How many US paper banknotes were in circulation at the end of 2023?
sourceName: Federal Reserve · Currency in Circulation: Volume
context: All denominations, including notes held outside the United States; count notes, not their dollar value.
route: Estimate notes held in wallets, tills and cash reserves. Then allow for savings and the large quantity held overseas.
example: A domestic starting point of 330 million people × 50 notes each gives 16.5 billion. Business holdings and overseas cash can multiply that severalfold.
insight: Cash outside everyday wallets is a major part of the money supply.

question: How many US banknotes were printed in fiscal 2023?
sourceName: Bureau of Engraving and Printing · annual production
context: October 2022–September 2023. Count newly printed notes of all denominations, not their dollar value.
route: Estimate the stock of notes and their replacement life. Add growth in demand; do not assume every note is newly printed each year.
example: For example: 50 billion notes ÷ a 10-year average replacement life ≈ 5 billion notes/year. Lifetimes differ greatly by denomination.
insight: Printing mainly replaces worn notes and meets changes in demand; it is not the same as the total cash already circulating.

question: How long a line can a BIC Cristal pen write, on average, according to BIC’s 2024 campaign?
sourceName: BIC · Write more, buy less campaign
context: The manufacturer’s stated average writing distance for the Cristal; actual writing conditions vary.
route: Picture pages filled before a pen runs dry. Estimate lines per page and the distance the pen travels while forming each line of handwriting.
example: An illustrative estimate: 400 pages × 30 lines/page × 0.3 m of pen travel per written line ≈ 3.6 km. These are scale assumptions, not a test protocol.
insight: A few millilitres or less of ink can make a remarkably long, thin trail.

question: How many lightning flashes occur worldwide in an average second?
context: Include cloud-to-cloud and cloud-to-ground flashes. Use NOAA’s rounded satellite-based estimate.
route: Estimate how many thunderstorms are active at once and flashes per minute in an average storm. Most storms are not directly above you.
example: For example: 2,000 active storms × 1 flash/minute ÷ 60 ≈ 33 flashes/second. Storm intensity varies widely; this is a rough model.
insight: Flashes inside clouds count too, so ground-strike maps do not show the entire total.

question: How heavy was a fully fuelled Saturn V at liftoff?
context: Use NASA’s rounded figure for the Apollo rocket at launch.
route: Picture the rocket’s fuel tanks as tall cylinders. Estimate their combined volume and the mass of a cubic metre of dense liquid propellant. The empty structure and payload add more.
example: A cylinder roughly 10 metres wide and 30 metres tall holds over 2,000 cubic metres. At the density of water that would already weigh a couple of million kilograms. The real stages vary in size and use different propellants.
insight: The propellant accounts for much of the mass lifted at launch.

question: How much pressurised space is inside the International Space Station?
context: Use NASA’s approximate pressurised volume. Include habitable modules and other pressurised interiors.
route: Picture several rooms joined end to end. Use a typical module’s length and cross-section and count the pressurised modules. Leave solar panels and exterior trusses out.
example: Ten roughly cylindrical interiors, each about 4 metres across and 7 metres long, would contain around 880 cubic metres.
insight: The station’s exterior span says little about how much room the crew can occupy.

question: How far did the lunar rover travel during Apollo 17?
context: Total driving distance in the SP-4029 mission summary. Include all rover outings.
route: Estimate time spent driving rather than taking samples. Multiply by the speed of a small vehicle on rough terrain.
example: Four hours of driving at about 9 km/h would cover 36 km. The actual excursions included many stops for geology and experiments.
insight: Total distance driven can be much greater than the farthest point from the lander.

question: How much light-collecting area does the James Webb Space Telescope’s main mirror have?
context: Use NASA’s rounded collecting area for the segmented primary mirror.
route: Imagine the diameter of a large telescope mirror and work out the area of a circle that wide. Allow for the irregular outline and gaps in the segmented mirror.
example: A round disk 6 metres across has about 28 square metres of area. The mirror is assembled from hexagonal pieces with a different outline.
insight: Doubling mirror diameter would roughly quadruple light collection if the shape stayed the same.

question: How long did New Horizons take to reach Pluto from Earth?
context: Elapsed calendar days from launch to closest approach. The launch day counts as day zero.
route: Estimate how many Earth–Sun distances separate Earth and Pluto, then divide by how far a fast probe can travel per year.
example: At 15 km/s a probe covers about 470 million kilometres in a year. A several-billion-kilometre journey therefore takes years even at that speed.
insight: From January 19, 2006 to July 14, 2015, there were 3,463 elapsed calendar days.

question: How fast was Parker Solar Probe moving near its December 2024 closest approach to the Sun?
sourceName: NASA · Parker Solar Probe closest pass
context: Use NASA’s rounded speed relative to the Sun for the December 2024 pass.
route: Compare Earth’s orbital speed with a probe travelling much closer to the Sun. The characteristic orbital speed grows with the inverse square root of distance, and a fast flyby can be faster still.
example: If a spacecraft passes at one twentieth of Earth’s orbital distance, the local circular speed is about 4.5 times Earth’s 30 km/s. An eccentric orbit can raise the speed further.
insight: The record speed refers to the brief close approach, while the spacecraft moves more slowly farther from the Sun.
